As for the salt laws, loopholes and abuses emerge in myriad ways, yet the loss of tax quotas through the flight and migration of saltern households and the distress caused to merchants by illicit salt trafficking are the main issues. The key to rectifying this lies in the Censorial Officials holding the pivot at the top while strengthening the local authorities' power of inspection. Allotting leaching pits to produce salt is entirely for showing compassion to the saltern households; curbing smugglers and guarding against villains is entirely for facilitating the merchants' trade. For public salt quotas and illicit salt, the state has established statutes. What is essential is first to verify the adult males responsible for the quota production, and to reiterate and promulgate the orders for recruiting merchants. Households that have died out should promptly be investigated and exempted, while arrears should be recovered gradually. Even where people have scattered and migrated, the abandoned salt pans and old leaching pits must have been privately appropriated for personal enrichment by someone. Those willing to pay the taxes in compensation on their own should be permitted to do so; those willing…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
還本業者聽其私逸自便逃竈而爲民者
究之無少假也而內地私鬻者責之巡捕
海澨煽構者責之巡哨觸禁者盡法故縱
者連坐內可爲度支之助外可防嘯聚之
虞課漸完而商日益卽不必桑孔之平準
劉晏之常平財恒足也何憂乎鹽政之不
脩耶雖然此特就明問之所及者耳愚竊
有說焉傳曰有治人無治法書曰惟克果
斷乃罔後艱今粵中民力竭矣而山海之
===
寇猶然竊發卽欲去兵勢所不能其藉財
用非淺尠矣若徒執拘攣之見而狃於苟
安重疑畏之心而懈於責成則弊日益深
法日益廢脫有緩急斂民增賦不亦重其
困乎故愚以爲捄弊莫先任人而決斷之
機尤在加之意焉蓋清屯有專官捕鹽有
定職其責成非不詳且切矣顧一官而諸
司委焉一職而衆務紛焉一日作之十日
輟之辟十羊九牧道旁作舍縱才堪兼濟
punctuated: 還本業者聽。其私逸自便、逃竈而爲民者，究之無少假也。而內地私鬻者，責之巡捕；海澨煽構者，責之巡哨。觸禁者盡法，故縱者連坐。內可爲度支之助，外可防嘯聚之虞。課漸完而商日益，卽不必桑、孔之平準，劉晏之常平，財恒足也，何憂乎鹽政之不脩耶？雖然，此特就明問之所及者耳，愚竊有說焉。傳曰：「有治人，無治法。」《書》曰：「惟克果斷，乃罔後艱。」今粵中民力竭矣，而山海之寇猶然竊發。卽欲去兵，勢所不能，其藉財用非淺尠矣。若徒執拘攣之見，而狃於苟安；重疑畏之心，而懈於責成，則弊日益深，法日益廢。脫有緩急，斂民增賦，不亦重其困乎？故愚以爲捄弊莫先任人，而決斷之機，尤在加之意焉。蓋清屯有專官，捕鹽有定職，其責成非不詳且切矣。顧一官而諸司委焉，一職而衆務紛焉，一日作之，十日輟之，辟十羊九牧、道旁作舍，縱才堪兼濟，
translation_en:
… return to their original occupation, let them do so. As for those who secretly abscond for their own convenience, fleeing the salt-boiling households to become ordinary commoners, they should be investigated and prosecuted without the slightest leniency. Furthermore, responsibility for those peddling illicit salt in the interior should be assigned to the police patrols, while responsibility for those stirring up trouble along the sea coasts should be assigned to the maritime defense patrols. Those who violate the prohibitions should be punished to the full extent of the law, and those who intentionally let them go should be held jointly liable. Internally, this can serve as an aid to state finances; externally, it can guard against the danger of bandits banding together. As tax quotas are gradually fulfilled and merchants increasingly profit, even without the price-equalization (pingzhun) policies of Sang Hongyang 桑弘羊 and Kong Jin 孔僅 or the ever-normal (changping) system of Liu Yan 劉晏, wealth will constantly be sufficient—what worry would there be of the salt administration not being put in order?

Even so, this merely addresses what was covered in Your enlightened question; I humbly have something further to say. Tradition states: "There are governing men, not governing laws." The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Only by being able to make resolute decisions will there be no subsequent difficulties." Today in Guangdong (Yue), the strength of the people is exhausted, yet bandits in the mountains and on the seas still covertly erupt. Even if we wished to dispense with troops, circumstances make it impossible, and our reliance on financial resources is by no means slight. If we merely cling to narrow, rigid views and remain accustomed to a temporary peace, or harbor heavy doubts and fears and grow lax in holding officials accountable for results, then abuses will deepen day by day and the laws will fall into further disuse day by day. Should an emergency arise, extracting levies from the people and increasing taxes—would this not compound their distress? Therefore, I humbly consider that in remedying abuses nothing comes before entrusting the right men, and the pivot of resolute decision lies especially in paying close attention to this. Now, for clearing up military farm (tuntian) land there are dedicated officials, and for apprehending salt smugglers there are fixed posts; the manner of holding them accountable for results is neither unspecific nor lacking in urgency. Yet a single official receives commissions from multiple agencies, and a single post is entangled in a multitude of affairs. They work at it for one day and drop it for ten—like having nine herdsmen for ten sheep, or building a house by the roadside. Even if their talents were equal to managing multiple duties,…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
支吾且不暇安望其有成績耶惟在當事
者念
國計之重而思更化之難毅然以古法爲必
可復而不辭勞怨奮然以時弊爲必當革
而不阻權豪有司之職屯鹽者必以是考
課最而不得以他委妨其職掌武弁之管
屯哨者必以是專督責而必以季終等其
賞罰假之便宜寬以歲月俾軍有恒產竈
無舊逋則屯政肅而軍實充鹽法脩而邊
===
儲裕雖百世可行非獨今日已也先民有
言詢于芻蕘惟執事采擇焉
第五問
鄭育漸
同考試官教諭羅 批 兵食之畫士子類能條
之獨是篇鏡古籌今慮周計悉當於粵政有裨不
但文逼秦漢而已
考試官教諭楊 批 筆意高古條議精確錄
之
punctuated:
支吾且不暇，安望其有成績耶？惟在當事者念國計之重，而思更化之難，毅然以古法爲必可復，而不辭勞怨；奮然以時弊爲必當革，而不阻權豪。有司之職屯鹽者，必以是考課最，而不得以他委妨其職掌；武弁之管屯哨者，必以是專督責，而必以季終等其賞罰。假之便宜，寬以歲月，俾軍有恒產，竈無舊逋，則屯政肅而軍實充，鹽法脩而邊儲裕，雖百世可行，非獨今日已也。先民有言：「詢于芻蕘。」惟執事采擇焉。

第五問
鄭育漸
同考試官教諭羅批：兵食之畫，士子類能條之，獨是篇鏡古籌今，慮周計悉，當於粵政有裨，不但文逼秦漢而已。
考試官教諭楊批：筆意高古，條議精確，錄之。
translation_en:
…they do not even have time to muddle through, so how can one hope for them to achieve tangible results? It rests solely upon those in authority to bear in mind the gravity of the state's finances and reflect upon the difficulty of reforming governance—resolutely deeming the ancient laws as certainly recoverable without shirking toil or resentment, and boldly deeming current abuses as certainly requiring abolition without being deterred by the powerful and magnates. For civil officials whose duties lie in military colonies and the salt administration, their performance evaluations must be based on this, and other commissions must not be allowed to interfere with their responsibilities; for military officers who manage colony patrols, they must be held exclusively accountable for this, and their rewards and punishments must be graded on this basis at the end of every season. Grant them discretionary power and allow them ample months and years, so that the soldiers have permanent property and the saltern households have no old arrears. Then the administration of military colonies will be well-ordered and military provisions abundant, the salt laws will be restored and frontier reserves plentiful; this could be practiced even for a hundred generations, not merely today. The ancients had a saying: "Consult the grass and firewood gatherers." May Your Excellency select and adopt what is useful here.

Question Five
Zheng Yujian 鄭育漸
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Luo 羅: Plans regarding troops and provisions can generally be itemized by the candidates, yet this essay alone mirrors antiquity to plan for the present, with comprehensive forethought and thorough calculation. It should be of real benefit to the governance of Guangdong, not merely rivaling the prose of the Qin and Han dynasties.
Comment by Examiner Instructor Yang 楊: Its stylistic conception is lofty and ancient, and its itemized proposals are precise and sound. Record it.

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭朱　批　博學宏猷非淺學可到
執事以東粤兵食爲問愚經生耳安足與
計天下事雖然則甞聞之矣昔齊桓以良
車三百乗教卒萬人以爲兵首南伐至召
陵北伐山戎西伐大夏涉流沙束馬懸車
登太行至卑耳山横行天下莫之能禁晉
文造五兩之士五乗銳卒千人先以接敵
侵曹伐衞抑楚會盟踐土尊天子於雍諸
侯莫能難夫齊晉盟主攘夷尊周豈待漕
===
輓方輸轉道千里哉其名正其義順行令
中國所在傳食至其人徒之費多不滿萬
所謂城濮之戰晉師在楚三日榖者是矣
豈若後世謀詐用而從横長短之説起於
是有輕點烏合假道借食兵興數十萬而
用始絀是以無名之師無用之食聖人畏
之故兵不在多寡在於選練將不在勇怯
在於知兵國之大計不可不審也夫教笞
不可弛於家刑罰不可廢於國征伐不可
punctuated:
考試官教諭朱批：博學宏猷，非淺學可到。

執事以東粤兵食爲問，愚，經生耳，安足與計天下事？雖然，則甞聞之矣。昔齊桓以良車三百乗、教卒萬人，以爲兵首。南伐至召陵，北伐山戎，西伐大夏，涉流沙，束馬懸車，登太行，至卑耳山，横行天下，莫之能禁。晉文造五兩之士五乗，銳卒千人，先以接敵。侵曹伐衞，抑楚，會盟踐土，尊天子於雍，諸侯莫能難。夫齊、晉盟主，攘夷尊周，豈待漕輓方輸、轉道千里哉？其名正，其義順，行令中國，所在傳食，至其人徒之費，多不滿萬。所謂城濮之戰，晉師在楚三日榖者是矣。豈若後世謀詐用而從横長短之説起，於是有輕點烏合，假道借食，兵興數十萬而用始絀。是以無名之師、無用之食，聖人畏之。故兵不在多寡，在於選練；將不在勇怯，在於知兵。國之大計，不可不審也。夫教笞不可弛於家，刑罰不可廢於國，征伐不可
translation_en:
Examiner and Instructor Zhu's comment: "Broad learning and grand plans, beyond the reach of shallow scholarship."

Your Excellency has inquired about military forces and food supplies in Eastern粵 (Guangdong). I am merely a student of the classics; how could I be worthy of discussing the affairs of the empire with you? Even so, I have heard something of the matter. In antiquity, Duke Huan of Qi used three hundred fine chariots and ten thousand trained foot soldiers as the vanguard of his army. In the south, he campaigned as far as Shaoling; in the north, he attacked the Mountain Rong; in the west, he campaigned against Daxia and crossed the Flowing Sands; binding his horses and slinging up his chariots, he ascended the Taihang Mountains and reached Mount Bei'er, ranging across the world with no one able to stop him. Duke Wen of Jin organized five chariots of warriors in five-squad formations and a thousand elite troops to be the first to engage the enemy. He invaded Cao and attacked Wei, checked Chu, convened the covenant at Jiantu, and honored the Son of Heaven at Yong, with none of the feudal lords able to challenge him. Now, when the leaders of the covenants of Qi and Jin repelled the barbarians and honored the Zhou royal house, did they have to wait for grain to be shipped by canal or carted in square convoys over supply routes of a thousand li? Their cause was legitimate and their righteousness was in accord with principle; when they issued commands across the Central States, they were provisioned by relay wherever they went, and as for the expense in men and followers, at most it did not reach ten thousand. What is spoken of in the Battle of Chengpu—that the Jin army lived off Chu's grain for three days—is an example of this. How could this be like later ages, when deceitful stratagems came into use and the theories of vertical and horizontal alliances and of manipulation arose, whereupon there were rashly conscripted, motley crowds borrowing passage and begging for provisions, raising armies of several hundred thousand until resources finally ran short? Therefore, an army without a legitimate cause and food consumed to no avail were things the sages feared. Thus, with soldiers, the issue lies not in whether they are many or few, but in selecting and training them; with generals, it lies not in whether they are brave or timid, but in their understanding of warfare. In the great plans of the state, one cannot fail to examine this carefully. Now, instruction and the rod cannot be relaxed in a household, punishments and penalties cannot be abolished in a state, and punitive expeditions cannot…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
偃於天下施之有順逆行之有次第而法
曰以逸待勞勝以虞待不虞勝又曰以飽
待饑勝夫千里饋糧士有饑色師不宿飽
難與應敵故兵不如者勿與挑戰粟不如
者勿與持乆此言食之爲重也長平之戰
秦以輕兵遮趙食而括斃河北之軍築甬
道輸之粟項羽渡河九戰絕之虜王離破
秦軍沛公竝兵而西高陽生仗策襲陳留
得積粟入關驃騎從軍天子至遣大官齎
===
數十乘重車餘梁肉如此其備也夫師行
糧食蓋自古記之今公私所汲汲而苦不
贍者其究安在或曰在兵而不在食愚則
曰在食而不在兵當事者徒循莫爲善後
之計而愚竊有惑也夫以粵之寥邈民疲
於作業農桑之事罕焉然以司府之兵食
計之歲入不下四十二萬惠潮之間曠土
千里惟正之負輸尚數十萬以其所入給
其所出而又取盈於常供游食之待哺者
punctuated: 偃於天下，施之有順逆，行之有次第。而法曰：「以逸待勞勝，以虞待不虞勝。」又曰：「以飽待饑勝。」夫千里饋糧，士有饑色，師不宿飽，難與應敵。故兵不如者，勿與挑戰；粟不如者，勿與持乆，此言食之爲重也。長平之戰，秦以輕兵遮趙食而括斃；河北之軍，築甬道輸之粟，項羽渡河九戰絕之，虜王離、破秦軍；沛公竝兵而西，高陽生仗策襲陳留，得積粟入關；驃騎從軍，天子至遣大官齎數十乘，重車餘梁肉，如此其備也。夫師行糧食，蓋自古記之。今公私所汲汲而苦不贍者，其究安在？或曰：在兵而不在食。愚則曰：在食而不在兵。當事者徒循，莫爲善後之計，而愚竊有惑也。夫以粵之寥邈，民疲於作業，農桑之事罕焉。然以司府之兵食計之，歲入不下四十二萬。惠、潮之間，曠土千里，惟正之負輸尚數十萬。以其所入給其所出，而又取盈於常供，游食之待哺者…
translation_en: …cease throughout the realm; in applying them there is proper order and reversal, and in carrying them out there is sequence and degree. The military canons state: "To await the exhausted in ease brings victory; to await the unprepared in readiness brings victory." They also say: "To await the hungry while well-fed brings victory." Indeed, when grain is transported for a thousand li, the soldiers wear a look of hunger; if an army does not have a full meal overnight, it is difficult to engage the enemy. Therefore, if one's troops are inferior, do not provoke battle; if one's grain is inferior, do not engage in a protracted standoff. This speaks to the paramount importance of provisions. At the Battle of Chang平 (Changping), Qin used light troops to intercept the provisions of Zhao, and Zhao Kuo 趙括 perished. For the army north of the Yellow River, a walled corridor was built to transport grain to it; Xiang Yu 項羽 crossed the river, cut the supply line in nine battles, captured Wang Li 王離, and shattered the Qin army. When the Duke of Pei 沛公 combined his forces and marched west, the scholar of Gaoyang 高陽生 (Li Yiji 酈食其) relied on a stratagem to make a surprise attack on Chenliu 陳留, securing its stockpiled grain before entering the Pass. When the General of Agile Cavalry (Piaoji jiangjun 驃騎將軍, Huo Qubing 霍去病) went on campaign, the Son of Heaven went so far as to dispatch the Grand Provisioner (Taiguan 大官) to bring dozens of carriages of supplies, so that the heavy baggage wagons had a surplus of fine grain and meat—such was the thoroughness of their preparation! That an army marches on its grain provisions has indeed been recorded since antiquity. Today, both public and private resources are anxiously strained and suffer from insufficiency—where does the root of this problem ultimately lie? Some say it lies in troops and not in food; I, however, say it lies in food and not in troops. Those in authority merely follow routine without devising a plan for future rehabilitation, and I am privately perplexed by this. Given the remoteness and vastness of Guangdong (Yue 粵), the people are exhausted by their livelihoods, and the pursuits of agriculture and sericulture are rare. Yet if we reckon the military provisions of the provincial administration commission and the prefectures, the annual revenue is no less than 420,000 [piculs/taels]. Between Huizhou 惠州 and Chaozhou 潮州, uncultivated land stretches for a thousand li, and the arrears in regular tax deliveries still amount to several hundred thousand. If we use what is taken in to supply what is paid out, while also demanding a full quota beyond the regular provisions, and the idle consumers waiting to be fed…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
嗷嗷然誰何此其難可知矣稱兵之後死
事之民不得一算之復議者見邊烽不驚
遂欲倣古寓兵於農之意嗟乎寢兵之說
勝則阻險不守矣兵民之說岐則士卒不
戰矣以其食之不給也而因以廢兵何異
因噎而廢食因溺而廢舟者乎故陸兵以
待萑葦之竊發水兵以待島嶼之出沒規
制華夷遏鎮要害缺一不可至其慎功實
之辨去浮淫之蠹防冒濫之原不可不察
===
也說者謂今之兵將非昔矣選練矣服習
矣其節約明矣步伐合地宜矣而執事猶
有不然者何耶夫明者視於無形聰者聽
於無聲誠先其未然則天下事無足爲者
今試舉一歲之所入而覈其所出其果一
一中食而無游靡者乎民之出食果足歲
計而無單竭抑損者乎官持尺籍料量果
鱗次輻輳無壅蹙於將事者乎田租河渡
鹽鐵榷會其果時入而不乾沒於胥吏逋
punctuated:
嗷嗷然誰何，此其難可知矣。稱兵之後，死事之民不得一算之復，議者見邊烽不驚，遂欲倣古寓兵於農之意。嗟乎！寢兵之說勝，則阻險不守矣；兵民之說岐，則士卒不戰矣。以其食之不給也，而因以廢兵，何異因噎而廢食、因溺而廢舟者乎？故陸兵以待萑葦之竊發，水兵以待島嶼之出沒，規制華夷，遏鎮要害，缺一不可。至其慎功實之辨，去浮淫之蠹，防冒濫之原，不可不察也。

說者謂今之兵將非昔矣，選練矣，服習矣，其節約明矣，步伐合地宜矣，而執事猶有不然者，何耶？夫明者視於無形，聰者聽於無聲，誠先其未然，則天下事無足爲者。今試舉一歲之所入而覈其所出：其果一一中食而無游靡者乎？民之出食，果足歲計而無單竭抑損者乎？官持尺籍料量，果鱗次輻輳、無壅蹙於將事者乎？田租、河渡、鹽鐵、榷會，其果時入而不乾沒於胥吏、逋
translation_en:
… clamor hungrily—what can be done about them? From this, the difficulty of the situation is evident. After the outbreak of hostilities, the people who died in service did not even receive exemption from a single poll tax; yet commentators, seeing that the frontier beacons are currently undisturbed, wish to imitate the ancient principle of lodging the military among the peasantry. Alas! When arguments for disarming prevail, strategic passes and defiles go unguarded; when views on separating or merging soldiers and civilians diverge, the troops cease to fight. To abolish the military simply because provisions are insufficient—how is that any different from giving up eating for fear of choking, or abolishing boats because someone has drowned? Therefore, land forces are needed to guard against bandits secretly springing from the reed marshes, and naval forces are needed to watch against raiders appearing and disappearing among the islands. In regulating Chinese and non-Chinese alike and garrisoning strategic chokepoints, neither can be dispensed with. As for carefully distinguishing genuine merit, eliminating the parasites of extravagance and excess, and guarding against the sources of fraudulent claims and abuses, these matters must be thoroughly examined.

Some argue that today's troops and commanders are no longer what they were in the past: they have been selected and trained, they are accustomed to service, their discipline and restraint are clear, and their maneuvers suit the terrain. Why, then, does Your Excellency still find this unsatisfactory? Now, the clear-sighted perceive what has not yet taken form, and the keen-eared hear what has not yet made a sound; if one truly anticipates matters before they materialize, then nothing in the realm is difficult to manage. Let us now take the revenues of a single year and verify them against the expenditures: does every single portion truly go to feed the troops without being squandered on idle waste? Are the provisions contributed by the people truly sufficient for the annual budget without exhausting and depleting them? Do the officials holding the military registers and measuring out grain supplies truly gather and distribute them in orderly succession, without bottlenecks or shortages when operations are underway? And do the land taxes, river-crossing tolls, salt and iron revenues, and commercial excises truly come in on time, without being embezzled by petty clerks or evaded and…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
貸於豪富者乎彼其林林相聚星羅碁布
爲其先於無形而制其未動也枵腹而待
則良平失其智衞霍無所策彼之視我如
振落我之視彼如赴湯火是我制於敵而
不能制敵進退之權皆不在我其去來任
之矣然則所云兵將水陸者其聲實安在
乎古者兵民不分無事則耰鋤良民有事
則荷戈接敵故軍興不煩均節而九賦九
式無所謂兵旅之費今兵民二而緩急無
===
所恃羽書狎至所調發不逮千數邦內騷
動有司屛營旁皇日饔月餼行饟坐餉袖
手待絀主將齮齕所謂民外之兵不耕而
食者其不能贍勢也吾觀漢將以雲中守
却匈奴七百餘里虜不敢南下牧馬今得
爲漢故事乎守自守而將自將故將得調
其攻殺刺擊而不得適饑飽其有所掣肘
而不能專制者亦勢也又况兵力有不盡
然者此民所以囂囂苦不足也分屯列戍
punctuated: 貸於豪富者乎？彼其林林相聚，星羅碁布，爲其先於無形而制其未動也。枵腹而待，則良、平失其智，衞、霍無所策，彼之視我如振落，我之視彼如赴湯火。是我制於敵而不能制敵，進退之權皆不在我，其去來任之矣。然則所云兵將水陸者，其聲實安在乎？古者兵民不分，無事則耰鋤良民，有事則荷戈接敵，故軍興不煩均節，而九賦九式無所謂兵旅之費。今兵民二而緩急無所恃，羽書狎至，所調發不逮千數，邦內騷動，有司屛營旁皇，日饔月餼，行饟坐餉，袖手待絀，主將齮齕。所謂民外之兵，不耕而食者，其不能贍，勢也。吾觀漢將以雲中守却匈奴七百餘里，虜不敢南下牧馬，今得爲漢故事乎？守自守而將自將，故將得調其攻殺刺擊，而不得適饑飽，其有所掣肘而不能專制者，亦勢也。又况兵力有不盡然者，此民所以囂囂苦不足也。分屯列戍
translation_en:
… owed in arrears by the wealthy and powerful? That they gather in multitudes, arrayed like stars in the sky or pieces on a go board, is so that we may anticipate the enemy before they take form and control them before they make a move. Yet if our troops wait on empty stomachs, then even Zhang Liang 張良 and Chen Ping 陳平 would lose their wisdom, and Wei Qing 衛青 and Huo Q病霍去病 would have no strategy to employ; the enemy would view us as easily shaken off as falling leaves, while we would view them as if walking into boiling water or fire. Thus we would be controlled by the enemy rather than able to control them; the initiative to advance or retreat would not rest with us at all, and they could come and go as they please. That being so, where is the reality behind the reputation of what we call our generals, troops, and land and naval forces?

In antiquity, soldiers and civilians were not separated. In times of peace, they were good subjects wielding hoes and rakes; in times of crisis, they shouldered spears to engage the enemy. Therefore, military mobilizations did not require the trouble of equalizing and economizing supplies, and among the nine categories of revenue and nine formulas of expenditure, there was nothing called military expenses. Today, soldiers and civilians are divided into two, and yet in emergencies there is nothing to rely upon. When urgent dispatches arrive one after another, even before the troops mobilized reach a thousand in number, the entire region is thrown into turmoil. The authorities pace back and forth in anxious bewilderment over daily rations and monthly provisions, supplies for campaigning and pay for garrisoning; they fold their hands and wait for funds to run out, while the commanding generals clash and bicker. That these so-called soldiers outside the civilian population—who eat without plowing—cannot be adequately supported is simply the inevitable trend of circumstances.

I observe that in the Han dynasty, generals serving as Grand Administrators of Yunzhong 雲中 drove back the Xiongnu 匈奴 by more than seven hundred li, so that the raiders dared not come south to pasture their horses. Can we follow that Han precedent today? Today, civil administrators manage their own jurisdictions while generals command their own troops; thus a general may direct the attacking, killing, thrusting, and striking, but cannot regulate the troops' hunger or fullness. That their hands are tied and they cannot exercise sole authority is also the inevitable trend of circumstances. How much more so when the strength of the troops is not even fully as claimed! This is why the people clamor in distress over insufficiency. Since the method of dividing agricultural colonies and arraying frontier garrisons…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之法既不能如古而雜耕渭濱之事兵又
不肯屈首就信地以稍寬民力吾知司計
者有不能一夕高枕矣然則故額不可增
也量入而出計口而授其有司之事乎程
其武力嚴其節制省其技擊必其賞罰其
將帥事乎先後虛實雲物風候陰符直經
之類羣七校之士而聽命不使有一夫偷
靡焉則將知兵兵習戰攻則取守則固懷
敵附遠何招不至兵得以保境民得以脩
===
業兵民相用百世之利也管子曰國不虛
重兵不虛勝民不虛用令不虛行國重以
兵兵勝在民民用以令令行以財今嶺海
之民疲矣正賦之外所輸幾何縣官之督
促無已入不及十分之一而云終歲勤動
其厭兵者一切偷安目前曰無事見兵而
不見敵有事見敵而不見兵寧蠲四十萬
之輸使民自戰守彼雖善攻終不能歲得
四十萬我即不善守終不至歲失四十萬
punctuated: 之法既不能如古，而雜耕渭濱之事，兵又不肯屈首就信地，以稍寬民力，吾知司計者有不能一夕高枕矣。然則故額不可增也。量入而出，計口而授，其有司之事乎？程其武力，嚴其節制，省其技擊，必其賞罰，其將帥事乎？先後虛實、雲物風候、陰符直經之類，羣七校之士而聽命，不使有一夫偷靡焉，則將知兵，兵習戰。攻則取，守則固，懷敵附遠，何招不至？兵得以保境，民得以脩業，兵民相用，百世之利也。管子曰：「國不虛重，兵不虛勝，民不虛用，令不虛行。國重以兵，兵勝在民，民用以令，令行以財。」今嶺海之民疲矣。正賦之外，所輸幾何？縣官之督促無已，入不及十分之一，而云終歲勤動。其厭兵者，一切偷安目前，曰：「無事見兵而不見敵，有事見敵而不見兵。寧蠲四十萬之輸，使民自戰守。彼雖善攻，終不能歲得四十萬；我即不善守，終不至歲失四十萬。」
translation_en:
…cannot match those of antiquity, and as for the practice of farming interspersed with the locals along the banks of the Wei River, the soldiers are furthermore unwilling to bow their heads and take to their assigned lands so as to slightly relieve the strength of the people. I know that those in charge of fiscal planning cannot rest easy on their pillows for even a single night! If that is so, then the original quotas cannot be increased. Measuring expenditures against revenues and doling out rations by counting mouths—is that not the business of the civil authorities? Assessing their martial strength, enforcing strict discipline, inspecting their combat skills, and making sure of rewards and punishments—is that not the business of the generals and commanders? As for matters such as priority and sequence, emptiness and solidity, cloud formations and wind portents, the Secret Tally (Yinfu) and the Direct Classic [? zhi jing], if one gathers the troops of the seven regiments to obey commands without allowing a single man to be remiss or wasteful, then the generals will know their troops, and the troops will be practiced in warfare. When attacking they will capture, and when defending they will hold firm; in winning over enemies and attracting the distant, who will not come when summoned? The soldiers will be able to protect the borders, and the common people will be able to pursue their livelihoods; soldiers and civilians mutually supporting one another is a benefit for a hundred generations.

Guanzi said: "A state is not weighty in vain, troops are not victorious in vain, the people are not employed in vain, and orders are not carried out in vain. A state is weighty through its troops, troops are victorious through the people, the people are employed through orders, and orders are carried out through wealth." Today, the people of the Linghai region [Guangdong] are exhausted. Beyond the regular tax quota, how much more do they contribute? The pressing and urging of the county magistrates never ends; what is brought in does not reach one-tenth, and yet the people are kept toiling the whole year round. Those who are weary of the military all seek temporary ease for the present moment, saying: "In times of peace we see soldiers and do not see the enemy; in times of trouble we see the enemy and do not see soldiers. Better to remit the contribution of four hundred thousand and let the people fight and defend for themselves. Even if the enemy is good at attacking, in the end they cannot gain four hundred thousand a year; even if we are not good at defending, in the end we will not lose four hundred thousand a year."…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
强在俛仰之間故兵不足則召募之耳食
不足則徴發之耳此不過在股掌之上非
阨塞祕伏而籌也至於兵不習戰以其將
予敵將不知兵以其國予敵嚴矣哉然則
桓文之兵可謂入其域而有節制者而猶
不足以敵湯武之仁義則所云技擊銳士
又在桓文下矣若今之士去秦魏又下矣
吾故曰兵不在多寡而在選練將不在勇
怯而在知兵書生何知鄰於狂瞽惟執事
===
裁擇
punctuated: 强在俛仰之間，故兵不足則召募之耳，食不足則徴發之耳。此不過在股掌之上，非阨塞祕伏而籌也。至於兵不習戰，以其將予敵；將不知兵，以其國予敵。嚴矣哉！然則桓、文之兵，可謂入其域而有節制者，而猶不足以敵湯、武之仁義，則所云技擊、銳士，又在桓、文下矣；若今之士，去秦、魏又下矣。吾故曰：兵不在多寡，而在選練；將不在勇怯，而在知兵。書生何知，鄰於狂瞽，惟執事裁擇。
translation_en: … [weakness and] strength can change in the blink of an eye. Therefore, if soldiers are insufficient, one simply recruits them; if provisions are insufficient, one simply requisitions them. This is merely a matter kept in the palm of one's hand, not something devised in desperate straits or secret hiding. As for the saying, "When soldiers are not trained in warfare, it is handing their general over to the enemy; when a general does not understand warfare, it is handing his state over to the enemy"—how stern that is! Thus, the troops of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin could be said to have entered the realm of disciplined forces, yet they were still no match for the benevolence and righteousness of Tang and Wu. Then those spoken of as skilled strikers (jiji) and sharp warriors (ruishi) were even inferior to the troops of Huan and Wen; and as for the soldiers of today, they are even further below those of Qin and Wei. Therefore I say: the effectiveness of troops lies not in their numbers, but in their selection and training; the worth of a general lies not in his bravery or cowardice, but in his understanding of warfare. What does a mere scholar know? My words border on the rash and blind; I only beg Your Excellency to judge and select from them.

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
此其尤章明較著者也然天生五材誰能
去兵國家雖平忘戰必危自古及今未有
易者是故嚴覈實而舟游之師虛實相半
矣則冒名之罰宜重也精武技而貴游之
子濫竽行列矣則浮冗之禁宜亟也謹斥
堠而信地之別依違觀望矣則失事之罪
宜正也戒姑息而脅從之黨哨聚要賞矣
則招撫之失宜究也兵以禦備而偏將裨
將人奴役使矣則點閱之法宜慎也而又
===
為之慎召募覈功實撫民不以入士伍謁
客不以待行間試之以刺擊而陰簡其白
徒不必補可也均之以營伍而稍減其名
額數不必六可也專之以責任而統之以
裨將遥授名色之類不必多可也縱賊與
退縮同罰頂名與失事同罰起居不精動
靜不必士不選練卒不服習則將領同罰
如此則民之營衛也國之屏蔽也彼其食
之也奚尤焉雖然兵凶器戰危事以弱為
punctuated: 此其尤章明較著者也。然天生五材，誰能去兵？國家雖平，忘戰必危，自古及今，未有易者。是故嚴覈實，而舟游之師虛實相半矣，則冒名之罰宜重也；精武技，而貴游之子濫竽行列矣，則浮冗之禁宜亟也；謹斥堠，而信地之別依違觀望矣，則失事之罪宜正也；戒姑息，而脅從之黨哨聚要賞矣，則招撫之失宜究也；兵以禦備，而偏將裨將人奴役使矣，則點閱之法宜慎也。而又為之慎召募，覈功實，撫民不以入士伍，謁客不以待行間；試之以刺擊，而陰簡其白徒，不必補可也；均之以營伍，而稍減其名額，數不必六可也；專之以責任，而統之以裨將，遥授名色之類，不必多可也。縱賊與退縮同罰，頂名與失事同罰，起居不精，動靜不必，士不選練，卒不服習，則將領同罰。如此，則民之營衛也，國之屏蔽也，彼其食之也奚尤焉？雖然，兵，凶器；戰，危事。以弱為
translation_en: …These are the most glaringly obvious cases. Yet Heaven gave birth to the five materials—who can do away with weapons? Though the state be at peace, to forget warfare inevitably brings peril; from antiquity to the present, this truth has never changed. Therefore, although we strictly verify the facts, the naval and roving forces are still half nominal and half real, so the punishment for fraudulent impersonation ought to be made heavy; although we seek to refine martial skills, the sons of noble and well-connected families still pad the ranks without merit, so the prohibition against superfluous personnel ought to be made urgent; although we take care with scouting and outposts, the division of assigned defense sectors still leads to hesitation and watching from the sidelines, so the crime of dereliction in military affairs ought to be rectified; although we warn against indulgent leniency, coerced followers still gather in bands to demand rewards, so the failures of pacification policies ought to be investigated; and although troops are meant for defense, Assistant Commanders and Lieutenant Generals treat them as personal servants and slaves, so the methods of roll-call and inspection ought to be made rigorous. Furthermore, we should be cautious in recruitment and verify actual merit, not inducting pacified rebels into the ranks of soldiers, nor entertaining visiting patronage-seekers in the military camps; we may test them in thrusting and striking and quietly weed out the untrained men, without necessarily replacing them; we may equalize the camp units and slightly reduce their nominal quotas, without the number necessarily having to be six; we may concentrate responsibility and place them under the command of Lieutenant Generals, without needing to multiply titular or remotely conferred appointments. Letting bandits escape should be punished the same as retreating in cowardice; substituting names on the rosters should be punished the same as failing in duty; and if routine discipline is not sharp, if movements are not decisive, if officers are not selected and trained, and if soldiers are not accustomed and drilled, then the commanders should share the same punishment. If this is done, then the troops will be the protective guard of the people and the defensive screen of the state—what fault could there be in their eating the state's rations? Even so, weapons are instruments of ill omen, and warfare is a perilous affair. Taking weakness as…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
廣東鄉試錄後序
萬曆四年秋八月廣東鄉試
錄成重俊以職事次當授簡
乃敬颺言曰美哉人文斌斌
盛矣以此獻
上庶幾先資之言哉雖然多士亦
知其所以有
===
今日者乎粵故濱海去天萬里
禹跡所不踐聲敎曰曁冒之
而已方漢之隆也粵人阻嶮
以與上國亢衡至勤樓船下
瀨之師堇能一之最後珠厓
置郡以議不便旋罷蓋其遠
而難馴也如此此何暇黌序
punctuated:
廣東鄉試錄後序

萬曆四年秋八月，《廣東鄉試錄》成，重俊以職事次當授簡，乃敬颺言曰：美哉人文，斌斌盛矣！以此獻上，庶幾先資之言哉！雖然，多士亦知其所以有今日者乎？粵故濱海，去天萬里，禹跡所不踐，聲敎曰曁，冒之而已。方漢之隆也，粵人阻嶮以與上國亢衡，至勤樓船、下瀨之師，堇能一之。最後珠厓置郡，以議不便，旋罷。蓋其遠而難馴也如此，此何暇黌序
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Guangdong Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the fourth year of the Wanli reign (1576), the Record of the Guangdong Provincial Examination was completed. By the order of my official duties, it fell to me, Chongjun, to take up the brush. I therefore respectfully proclaim: How splendid is this literary culture, how refined and flourishing! In presenting this to His Majesty, may these words serve as an initial pledge of service! Even so, do you gentlemen also know how it is that you have come to see this day?

Guangdong borders the sea, ten thousand li distant from the imperial court. It was a place untrodden by the footsteps of Yu; when it was said that prestige and teachings reached it, they merely covered it loosely from above. At the height of the Han dynasty, the people of Guangdong relied on their rugged terrain to contend against the central state, to the point that it required the exertion of the Tower-Ship and Rapid-Current generals before the region could barely be unified. Later on, when Zhuya was established as a commandery, it was soon abolished following deliberations over its inconvenience. Such was the extent to which the region was remote and difficult to tame—what leisure was there for the affairs of schools…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之事賓興之舉乎爰及唐宋
文獻乃可徵然亦堇堇指數
皇明受
天景命南嚮而聽所漸摩覆露無
先于南者粤自是蔚爲文明
之區矣考科目得人則莫若
弘正之際與嘉靖初元雖立
===
功立德所究人人殊總之弗
遜于古頃粤乂稱兵士惴焉
未有寧宇賴
朝廷威靈山妖海孽以次芟夷
蘊崇之昔之贏糧而入保者
今得鼓篋而復脩其業矣則
何莫非
punctuated: 之事，賓興之舉乎？爰及唐、宋，文獻乃可徵，然亦堇堇指數。皇明受天景命，南嚮而聽，所漸摩覆露，無先于南者，粤自是蔚爲文明之區矣。考科目得人，則莫若弘、正之際與嘉靖初元；雖立功、立德，所究人人殊，總之弗遜于古。頃粤乂稱兵，士惴焉未有寧宇；賴朝廷威靈，山妖海孽，以次芟夷蘊崇之。昔之贏糧而入保者，今得鼓篋而復脩其業矣。則何莫非
translation_en: … the affairs [of schools] and the enterprise of recommending worthy talents? Coming down to the Tang and Song dynasties, literary documents and worthies could finally be attested, yet even then they could barely be counted on one's fingers. When the August Ming received the great mandate of Heaven and faced south to govern, in its gradual moral transformation and nurturing shelter, no region took precedence over the south; from this point on, Yue [Guangdong] flourished as a realm of civilization and culture. If we examine the talent obtained through the civil service examinations, no period matched the transition between the Hongzhi (1488–1505) and Zhengde (1506–1521) eras and the beginning of the Jiajing era (1522–1566). Although in establishing merit and establishing virtue each person's ultimate attainment differed, taken altogether they were in no way inferior to the ancients. Recently, warfare broke out again in Yue [? reading 乂 as 又/復], and the scholars were fearful and had no peaceful abode. Relying on the majesty and numinous power of the Imperial Court, the mountain demons and sea monsters [bandits and pirates] have one after another been mowed down, eradicated, and heaped up for destruction. Those who formerly carried provisions on their backs to take refuge in strongholds are now able to beat the drum, open their book-boxes, and resume their studies. How could any of this be anything other than…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
上恩哉故重俊竊伏讀多士之文
而知其盛之有自也夫攀翠
虯之逸鱗附朱鳳之靈羽出
渫離奧自燿于熙明者大人
之業也泳
玄澤戴
鴻施烝烝然思報效無已者烈士
===
之槩也多士旦夕躡屩而上
公車試用伊始且安所成信
乎粤言之與效實也則有異
矣志不幾于峻標峙坊而陽
浮以隨俗之好道不存于塞
違昭德而如韋以干主之澤
事不顓于詒法賴民而設色
punctuated: 上恩哉！故重俊竊伏讀多士之文，而知其盛之有自也。夫攀翠虯之逸鱗，附朱鳳之靈羽，出渫離奧，自燿于熙明者，大人之業也；泳玄澤、戴鴻施，烝烝然思報效無已者，烈士之槩也。多士旦夕躡屩而上公車，試用伊始，且安所成信乎？粤言之與效實也，則有異矣。志不幾于峻標峙坊，而陽浮以隨俗之好；道不存于塞違昭德，而如韋以干主之澤；事不顓于詒法賴民，而設色
translation_en: … His Majesty's grace! Thus, I, Chongjun, have humbly perused the essays of the many scholars and know that their flourishing has its origin. Now, to grasp the soaring scales of the emerald horned dragon and cling to the numinous plumes of the vermilion phoenix, emerging from obscurity and departing from seclusion to shine forth in an era of glorious brightness—this is the undertaking of a great man. To swim in profound beneficence and bear immense generosity above, ardently thinking of repaying the state without cease—this is the mettle of a heroic scholar. Soon the many scholars will put on their straw sandals and board the official carriages to the capital; as their probation and appointment begin, wherein will they establish their credibility? Indeed, there is a difference between uttering words and proving them in reality! When one's ambition does not aspire to set a lofty standard and stand as a moral bulwark, yet one puts on a superficial display to follow popular tastes; when one's Way does not lie in checking transgressions and manifesting virtue, yet one makes oneself pliable as soft leather to seek the ruler's favor; when one's service is not dedicated to bequeathing model laws and benefitting the people, yet one puts on a specious appearance…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
以要時之譽世所稱才賢大
率然已不者營私營利所如
滿志舉生平而弁髦之先資
謂何甚哉徒言之可畏也人
之材器固若升龠斗石然各
有所受不可强也乃如心無
不可自盡者是心之精潜深
===
入尠燭幽窮遐意有所注鬼
神輔之熊渠子援弓而射伏
石飲羽痀僂丈人承蜩猶掇
之也此精神之極也然心豈
有二用公私義利在决所擇
爾心乎爲私而能奉公心乎
爲利而能好義者無之故士
punctuated: 以要時之譽，世所稱才賢，大率然已。不者，營私營利，所如滿志，舉生平而弁髦之，先資謂何？甚哉，徒言之可畏也！人之材器，固若升龠斗石然，各有所受，不可强也。乃如心，無不可自盡者。是心之精，潜深入尠，燭幽窮遐，意有所注，鬼神輔之。熊渠子援弓而射，伏石飲羽；痀僂丈人承蜩，猶掇之也。此精神之極也。然心豈有二用？公私義利，在决所擇爾。心乎爲私而能奉公，心乎爲利而能好義者，無之。故士
translation_en: … putting on appearances to court contemporary acclaim—those whom the world calls talented and worthy are generally just like this. Otherwise, they pursue private ends and seek personal profit; getting their heart's desire wherever they go, they cast aside all their lifelong principles like a worn-out cap. What then becomes of the pledges with which they first paved their way to office? Dreadful indeed is empty talk! A person's talent and capacity are naturally like measures of a pint, a gill, a peck, or a picul—each has its own limit that cannot be forced. Yet when it comes to the mind, there is nothing in which one cannot fully exert oneself. The essence of this mind penetrates deeply into the subtlest realms, illuminating the obscure and reaching the distant; wherever its intent is focused, ghosts and spirits lend their aid. When Xiong Quzi drew his bow and shot, the crouching stone swallowed the fletching of his arrow; when the hunchbacked old man caught cicadas, it was as easy as picking them up from the ground. This is the utmost concentration of spirit. Yet how can the mind be applied in two directions at once? Between public and private, righteousness and profit, everything depends on making a decisive choice. There has never been anyone whose mind is set on private ends who can yet serve the public good, or whose mind is set on profit who can yet love righteousness. Therefore, if a scholar…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
誠服官思勤臨衆思辨在敵
思鬭銜命思不辱則盡心矣
心盡乃可以成信夫是之謂
眞才賢多士其無意不佞之
言乎繼自今以往永矢一心
以圖報塞勿以崇庳豐約多
岐岐之立功立德期有紹于
===
前聞使人謂科目得人無若
今玆爲最主司者亦竊知言
之名附于以人事
君之忠是士與主司耦俱得也昔
墨翟見素絲而歎曰此夫染
於蒼則蒼染於黃則黃者非
特物然士亦有之習俗之移
punctuated: 誠服官思勤，臨衆思辨，在敵思鬭，銜命思不辱，則盡心矣。心盡乃可以成信，夫是之謂眞才。賢多士其無意不佞之言乎？繼自今以往，永矢一心，以圖報塞，勿以崇庳豐約多岐岐之，立功立德，期有紹于前聞，使人謂科目得人無若今玆爲最。主司者亦竊知言之名，附于以人事君之忠，是士與主司耦俱得也。昔墨翟見素絲而歎曰：「此夫染於蒼則蒼，染於黃則黃者。」非特物然，士亦有之。習俗之移
translation_en: … truly think of diligence when serving in office, think of discernment when facing the multitude, think of fighting when confronting the enemy, and think of not bringing disgrace when bearing a commission, then they will have given their whole heart. Only when the heart is wholly given can trustworthiness be achieved; this is what is called true talent. Will the worthy scholars not heed these words of mine? From this day forward, forever swear to keep a single mind in seeking to repay the state; do not let yourselves be led astray along divergent paths by high or low rank, abundance or scarcity. In establishing merit and establishing virtue, aspire to carry on the renown of your predecessors, so that people will say that no recruitment by examination has ever surpassed the present one in obtaining capable men. Those in charge of the examination will also humbly claim a reputation for knowing men through their words, joining in the loyalty of serving the Sovereign by recommending worthy men. Thus both the scholars and the examiners will have achieved success together. In antiquity, Mo Di 墨翟 saw undyed silk and sighed, saying: "When this is dyed in blue, it becomes blue; when dyed in yellow, it becomes yellow." It is not only things that are so; scholars are subject to this as well. The way custom transforms…

title: 萬曆四年廣東鄉試錄
text:
人也甚於染多士始進宜自
愛母使命儒者爲墨氏之徒
所竊歎哉
浙江台州府僊居縣儒學敎
諭楊重俊謹序
punctuated:
人也，甚於染。多士始進，宜自愛，母使命儒者爲墨氏之徒所竊歎哉！
浙江台州府僊居縣儒學敎諭楊重俊謹序。
translation_en:
… men is worse than dyeing! As the many scholars first advance into office, they ought to cherish their own integrity—do not let those who call themselves Confucians be secretly lamented by the followers of Mozi!
Respectfully prefaced by Yang Chongjun 楊重俊, Instructor of the Confucian School (儒學教諭) of Xianju County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang.
